screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll build an intuitive understanding of UVs, the hidden bridge between your painted images and the surfaces of your 3D models. UVs are simply 2D coordinates—U across and V up—that map every point on a 3D mesh to a point on a flat texture. By the end you will be able to pick an appropriate initial projection, spot stretching, and plan safe seams for a clean UV layout. Ready to connect your 2D art to your 3D craft?

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Understanding UV Mapping Fundamentals

Why UVs matter: they let your detailed 2D textures wrap on complex 3D shapes without distortion. Learn how to unwrap, project, and arrange UVs for clean, game-ready assets.

Duration: ~10 min
In this lesson
UV basics, projections, editor, and common pitfalls.
Skills
Pick projections and spot stretching using a checker texture.
Outcome
Produce UV shells that fit the 0-1 space without overlap.
Explore Key Topics
Planar, cylindrical, spherical projections; 0-1 UV packing; avoiding stretching and overlap.
Visual Concept
0-1 UV space shown as a single square. UV shells must fit here for standard textures.
Why this matters

Proper UVs ensure consistent texel density, prevent overlaps that confuse baked maps, and let game engines sample textures efficiently.

Quick analogy

Unwrapping is like cutting cloth patterns for a garment. Each piece must be cut and arranged so printed details land where the designer intends.

Fourth, you will apply basic projection methods—planar, cylindrical, spherical—to appropriate geometry and recognize when a single projection will create distortion. Each objective includes a short explanation of why the skill matters: from achieving even texel density to avoiding overlapping shells that break baked maps. Finally, a small mnemonic for each objective links concept to practice so you can verify your competency in a real scene. By the end, you will be ready to apply these methods in a simple scene with a checker texture and assess quality quickly.

screens.title: Objectives — Practice & Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: These practice-focused objectives tell you how to verify results and what to avoid. First, learn to use a checkerboard material to visualize texel density and reveal stretching; the checker serves as a diagnostic tool so you can see where squares are elongated or compressed. Second, practice making seams and creating UV shells for complex models. Treat seams like tailoring cuts so pieces can flatten without significant distortion. Third, pack shells in the 0–1 space and watch for overlapping UVs that cause texture conflicts or incorrect baking. Overlap hides mistakes and breaks ambient occlusion or normal maps. Fourth, experiment with wrong projections deliberately — apply planar to a sphere or spherical to a cylinder — to see extreme distortion; this contrast helps you learn when each projection is appropriate. These objectives pair procedural practice with quick visual tests so you can iterate confidently. After these checks, you should be able to identify whether a texture problem is a projection choice, stretching, or overlapping, and pick a clear next step to fix it.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Practice & Pitfalls

Practice Checks and Common Pitfalls

Short practical tests that quickly tell you if your UVs are working.

Checker Test

Apply a dense checker texture and look for non-uniform squares to find stretching. Use repeat values like 10,10 for clarity.

Seams & Shells

Cut seams where necessary, create shells per logical parts, then unfold each shell with an appropriate projection to reduce distortion.

Packing

Scale and pack shells into the 0-1 square without overlaps to ensure correct texture sampling and clean baking results.

screens.title: What are UVs?
screens.narratorSegment: UVs are a mapping system: each vertex on a 3D model is assigned a pair of coordinates in a two-dimensional texture space called U and V. A useful mental image is peeling an orange or unwrapping a gift box so that the curved or folded surface becomes a flat piece of material you can paint on. When you paint in a 2D program, each pixel corresponds to some UV coordinate; the renderer looks up that pixel by reading the U and V assigned to the surface point. Concretely, U is the horizontal axis and V is the vertical axis of the texture map. Without that mapping, a 2D image has no way to know which triangle or vertex it should color on a model. A common beginner misconception is thinking UVs are the texture image: they are not. They are coordinates that reference the texture. An example: a character’s eye painted in 2D will only appear in the correct place on the head if the UVs for the eye region point to that painted region in the 0-1 space. Key takeaway: separate the idea of the texture image from the coordinate map that places it. Ask yourself when checking a model: is this a texture problem or a UV mapping problem?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: UVs are 2D coordinates assigned to 3D vertices that tell renderers where texture pixels should be sampled.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › What are UVs?
Definition

UV coordinates explained

UVs pair every 3D vertex with a point in 2D texture space so that images map correctly onto geometry. They do not contain color data themselves.

Analogy
Unwrapping a gift box or peeling an orange to lay the surface flat for painting.
Common misconception

UVs are not the texture image. They are the coordinate system that tells the texture where to appear on the mesh.

Key Takeaway

A correct UV map is the foundation for any texture to look right on a 3D model.

Concrete example

Imagine painting eyes in a 2D image. If the head’s UVs for the eye region point to that painted area within the 0-1 square, the eyes will appear correctly on the model. If they point elsewhere, the texture will not match the mesh’s intended features.

Check your understanding
  • Can you explain why UVs are needed even if you have a perfect texture image?
  • When might UVs be the root cause of misaligned details?

screens.title: The 0–1 UV Space
screens.narratorSegment: The 0–1 UV space is a normalized square that runs from U equals zero to U equals one and V equals zero to V equals one. This square represents the full extent of a single texture map. When artists paint in Photoshop or Substance, they assume artwork will be sampled across that square, so placing your UV shells inside 0–1 ensures the renderer fetches texture pixels predictably. For game workflows, keeping shells inside 0–1 makes atlasing and mipmapping straightforward and avoids sampling artifacts. Overlapping shells inside the 0–1 square can be intentional for mirrored symmetry, but accidental overlaps create conflicts: two different model parts will sample the same texture pixels, which breaks unique details and baked maps. A practical way to check texel distribution is to use a checker texture with repeated tiles; ideally the squares are uniformly sized across shells. A common mistake is allowing some shells to be tiny and others huge inside 0–1; that creates inconsistent texel density and visible variation in texture sharpness. Your practical rule: aim for even density and no accidental overlap inside the 0–1 square.

keyIdea.title: 0-1 space
keyIdea.text: The 0–1 square is the canonical texture area; shells inside it map to the texture; packing and scale control texel density and atlasing.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › 0–1 UV Space

The normalized UV square

This area defines the coordinates that a single texture occupies. Proper placement here affects sampling, mipmaps, and atlasing.

Packing & Texel Density

Scale shells so comparable parts share consistent texel density. Tiny shells yield blurry detail; oversized shells waste texture space.

Overlaps

Intentional overlaps can mirror symmetric details. Unintentional overlaps cause texture conflicts and baking errors.

Quick Tip

Use a tiled checker with repeat values to compare square sizes across shells rapidly.

Visual check
Good

Shells scaled and packed evenly, no overlap.

Problem

Tiny shell and a very large shell cause inconsistent detail and wasted space.

Check your understanding

If the left eye and right eye shells are overlapping algebraically in 0-1, what happens to unique eye detail in a painted texture?

screens.title: Navigating the UV Editor in Maya
screens.narratorSegment: The UV Editor is the primary workspace for arranging UVs in Maya. Open it from Windows, UV Editors, UV Editor. Inside, you can switch selection modes—UVs, edges, faces—so you can move individual coordinates, relax edges, or select whole shells. Transformation tools behave the same as in the 3D view: move, rotate, scale. One important habit is to use a checker texture on the model to evaluate stretching; irregular squares mean non-uniform mapping. The editor also shows the 0–1 square background and lets you nudge shells back into that square if they stray. A useful workflow is: isolate a shell, choose an appropriate projection, apply the projection manipulator to align the projection, then use transform tools and, if available, unfold or relax to reduce distortion. A common error is moving UVs without watching the model—always verify the viewport while editing. Example: after cylindrical mapping a bottle, rotate and scale the rectangular side shell in the UV Editor so its checker squares are square, then pack caps separately. That loop—project, adjust, verify—is the editor workflow you’ll practice. Navigating the UV Editor in Maya means select uv components, apply transforms, use a checker texture for visual feedback, and iterate: project, adjust, verify.. In practical terms, selection modes, transforms, and reading the checker view. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › UV Editor Workflow
Selection Modes
  • UV: move individual coordinates.
  • Edge: select island borders to cut or sew.
  • Face: project specific faces with mapping tools.
Workflow

Project → adjust with move/rotate/scale → relax/unfold → verify with checker → pack into 0-1.

Visual Diagnostic
Checker on model

Detect stretched or squashed areas immediately by looking at tile shapes on the 3D surface.

Projection manipulator

Align and scale the initial projection to minimize distortion before relaxing or unfolding.

Example

After cylindrical mapping a bottle, adjust the rectangular side shell so the checker squares are uniform, then rotate to align the seam where appropriate.

screens.title: Planar Projection
screens.narratorSegment: Planar projection flattens faces by projecting them along a single axis, like shining a flashlight perpendicular to a surface. It’s ideal for flat or mostly flat geometry such as walls, floors, or the side of a box. In Maya, select the faces or object, then choose UV, Planar Mapping and set Project From to the axis that best matches the surface orientation—Y axis for a horizontal plane, for example. Use the projection manipulator to position and scale the projected area so it covers the intended faces in the UV Editor. After projection, verify with a checker texture: the squares should be uniform and fill the 0–1 space appropriately. A common mistake is applying planar mapping to curved geometry like a sphere; that produces severe stretching and seams. A concrete example: Use planar mapping on a book cover by selecting the cover faces and projecting from the camera or axis perpendicular to the cover to produce a clean rectangular shell that maps to a flat texture image. Remember to scale and pack that shell into the 0–1 square for final texture painting.

keyIdea.title: Planar mapping
keyIdea.text: Project faces along one axis; best for flat surfaces. Verify with a checker and avoid using it on strongly curved geometry.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Planar Projection
When to use

Flat, single-direction surfaces

Best for walls, floors, and planar faces; quick and precise when the surface aligns with an axis.

Step-by-step
  1. Select faces or object.
  2. UV > Planar Mapping > set axis in options.
  3. Adjust the manipulator and scale in the UV Editor.
  4. Verify with a checker and pack into 0-1.
Example

Project a book cover from the front axis so the cover becomes a neat rectangle in the UV Editor ready for painting.

Common mistake

Applying planar mapping to curved geometry causes extreme stretching and visible seams.

Check

After projection, apply a checker with repeats of 10,10 and ensure tiles are uniform; if not, reposition or choose a different projection type.

screens.title: Cylindrical Projection
screens.narratorSegment: Cylindrical projection wraps the texture around an object’s circumference, making it ideal for bottles, trunks, arms, or tree trunks. Think of applying a label to a bottle: the label wraps cleanly around the sides but the end caps remain separate pieces. In Maya, select the object or faces and choose UV, Cylindrical Mapping. Set the projection axis—commonly Y for vertical cylinders—and use the manipulator to position the cylinder’s axis and radius so it aligns with the geometry. The UV Editor will typically show a rectangular shell for the side and circular shells for the caps. Check the checker texture: a properly mapped cylinder shows uniform squares on the side and may show stretching on the caps if they are left on the same projection. A typical pitfall is leaving caps attached to the side projection; instead, project caps separately or create dedicated shells for them. Example workflow: for a low-poly tree trunk, cylindrical-map the side, then planar-map the top and bottom caps so each region uses an appropriate projection and yields minimal distortion. Cylindrical Projection means best for tube-like geometry. wraps around circumference; separate caps into their own shells to reduce stretching.. In practical terms, wrapping textures around tube-like forms. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Cylindrical Projection

Use case and mechanics

Wraps textures like a label around the object. Adjust axis and radius with the manipulator for a clean unwrap.

Step-by-step
  1. Select faces or object.
  2. UV > Cylindrical Mapping > set axis (e.g., Y).
  3. Adjust manipulator to align radius and axis.
  4. Project caps separately if needed.
Practical Example

A tree trunk: cylindrical-map the bark region, planar-map the top and bottom to avoid pole distortion.

Issues to watch
  • Seam location where the wrap starts and ends may be visible; place seams where least noticeable.
  • Caps often need separate projections to avoid distortion at pole regions.
Check

Verify side tiles are square and seams are placed on non-prominent areas of the model.

screens.title: Spherical Projection
screens.narratorSegment: Spherical projection projects the surface from a sphere and is appropriate for dome-like geometry such as planets, heads, or round props. In Maya, select the object or faces and choose UV, Spherical Mapping. Set the projection axis—often Y—to center the sphere appropriately. After projecting, you’ll usually see a map with a seam and stretching near the poles: this is inherent to mapping a curved surface onto a flat plane. Use the checker texture to identify pinching at poles and consider splitting into shells or using additional seams to redistribute distortion. For a character head, for example, you might spherical-map the cranium but cut seams around the ears and jaw so you can create separate shells for the more detailed regions. A misconception is expecting a single spherical projection to produce zero distortion; instead, it provides an initial layout that you must refine. The rule of thumb is: use spherical for broad round areas and then adjust or split where detail requires less distortion. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Spherical Projection

Round forms and pole issues

Spherical maps suit broadly rounded objects but create stretching near poles that you must manage with seams and shells.

Example

Project a character’s cranium with spherical mapping, then cut out the ears and face into separate shells for detail control.

Common misconception

Expecting a perfect unwrap from spherical projection alone. It’s usually a starting point that needs refinement.

Practical checks
  • Look for pinching at top and bottom poles with a checker.
  • Consider splitting high-detail areas into their own shells.
Key Takeaway

Spherical mapping is useful but not final; refine seams to control distortion where detail matters.

screens.title: Projection Comparison: Planar vs Cylindrical vs Spherical
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the correct projection type is an early decision that shapes the rest of your UV workflow. Planar projection is best for flat or largely planar surfaces; it gives clean rectangular shells but fails badly on curved geometry, producing extreme stretching. Cylindrical mapping wraps around tube-like forms and handles side walls well, but tends to leave caps and seam edges that need separate attention. Spherical mapping is for dome-like shapes; it gives an intuitive cranium-style layout but commonly produces pole distortion. A helpful strategy is to compare results with a checker texture: apply each projection to the same model and observe where the checker tiles stay square. Example: try planar on a sphere and you’ll see dramatic stretching—this contrast teaches you what not to do. Another example: cylindrical on a bottle gives a neat side rectangle but leaves cap circles; you should then project caps separately or planar-map them. The key decision pattern: match projection geometry to model curvature, then split complicated parts into separate shells for tailored projection and packing. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Planar projection is best for flat or largely planar surfaces; it gives clean rectangular shells but fails badly on curved geometry, producing extreme stretching. Cylindrical mapping wraps around tube-like forms and handles side walls well, but tends to leave caps and seam edges that need separate attention. Spherical mapping is for dome-like shapes; it gives an intuitive cranium-style layout but commonly produces pole distortion. A helpful strategy is to compare results with a checker texture: apply each projection to the same model and observe where the checker tiles stay square. Example: try planar on a sphere and you’ll see dramatic stretching—this contrast teaches you what not to do. Another example: cylindrical on a bottle gives a neat side rectangle but leaves cap circles; you should then project caps separately or planar-map them. screens.title: Stretching and Overlapping
screens.narratorSegment: Stretching and overlapping are two frequent sources of texture failures. Stretching happens when the relationship between a 3D surface area and its 2D UV area is non-uniform, so texture pixels are squeezed or expanded unevenly. You can visualize stretching by applying a checker texture: elongated or squashed tiles tell you which regions need relaxation or a different projection. Overlapping occurs when two shells occupy the same spot in the 0–1 space. Overlap can be deliberate for mirrored textures, but accidental overlap causes different model parts to sample the same pixels and breaks unique details and baked maps. To fix stretching, try changing the projection, cutting seams to create new shells that can be unwrapped more naturally, or using relax/unfold tools to distribute UVs more evenly. To fix overlaps, select the shells and move or scale them apart, then repack into the 0–1 space. Example: a brick wall with stretched bricks likely has compressed UVs in the U direction; scale or reproject that area and check the tiles until the bricks appear proportionate. Always re-check in the viewport after adjustments. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Stretching & Overlap

Diagnose and fix UV problems

Stretching distorts texels; overlap causes texture conflicts. Both are visible with a checker and require targeted fixes.

Stretching symptoms

Elongated or squashed checker tiles. Fix by reprojecting, cutting seams, or relaxing the UVs.

Overlap symptoms

Two parts sample the same texture region. Fix by separating shells and repacking within 0-1.

Example

A brick texture appears squashed because that wall’s UVs were compressed horizontally; scaling the UVs restores correct brick proportions.

Key Takeaway

Use the checker as a diagnostic, then choose between reprojecting, cutting seams, or relaxing to fix stretching. Separate and repack to remove overlaps.

screens.title: Creating UV Shells and Cutting Seams
screens.narratorSegment: Complex models rarely unwrap well with a single projection. The solution is to cut seams and create UV shells—contiguous groups of UVs that unfold cleanly. Think like a tailor: identify logical part boundaries where seams are least visible, such as under an arm, inside a shoulder, or along the underside of a prop. In Maya, select edges to cut and use the appropriate UV > Cut or UV > Unfold tools; then pull apart the resulting shells in the UV Editor and apply suitable projections per shell. Each shell can be projected, relaxed, and scaled to maintain consistent texel density. For example, a character’s torso might be split into front and back shells, sleeves as cylindrical shells, and hands as separate shells to preserve detail. A common beginner mistake is cutting seams in highly visible areas; instead, plan seams where texture seams will be hidden by design or silhouette. Save incremental versions before aggressive cutting: complex UV edits can be tricky to undo. The practical outcome is smaller shells that unwrap with less distortion and pack efficiently into the 0–1 space.

screens.narratorSegment: Let’s summarize the most important ideas to keep in mind. First: UVs are coordinate pairs—U and V—that define how a 2D image maps onto a 3D surface. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll build an intuitive understanding of UVs, the hidden bridge between your painted images and the surfaces of your 3D models. UVs are simply 2D coordinates—U across and V up—that map every point on a 3D mesh to a point on a flat texture. Think of it as unwrapping a complex object and laying it flat so a painting program can color it correctly. You will learn the importance of the 0–1 UV square, how the UV Editor shows shells and islands, and why correct projection choices—planar, cylindrical, spherical—matter for different geometries. We’ll also cover common pitfalls: stretching, overlapping, and poor packing that ruin a texture in a game engine. Practically, you will see how to apply a checker texture to reveal distortions, how projection manipulators affect the initial unwrap, and why breaking a model into UV shells is like cutting fabric for a tailored garment. By the end you will be able to pick an appropriate initial projection, spot stretching, and plan safe seams for a clean UV layout. Ready to connect your 2D art to your 3D craft?

These objectives outline practical, measurable skills you will gain. First, you will define UVs and explain how U and V coordinates connect 2D textures to 3D surfaces. Being able to state this clearly helps you reason about texture placement and baking. Second, you will understand the 0–1 UV space: why all shells should live inside that square for standard texture maps and how packing affects memory and atlasing in games. Third, you will navigate Maya's UV Editor, select UVs, edges, and faces, and use move, rotate, and scale to improve layouts. This is a hands-on window where textures reveal stretching. Fourth, you will apply basic projection methods—planar, cylindrical, spherical—to appropriate geometry and recognize when a single projection will create distortion. Each objective includes a short explanation of why the skill matters: from achieving even texel density to avoiding overlapping shells that break baked maps. Finally, a small mnemonic for each objective links concept to practice so you can verify your competency in a real scene. By the end, you will be ready to apply these methods in a simple scene with a checker texture and assess quality quickly.

These practice-focused objectives tell you how to verify results and what to avoid. First, learn to use a checkerboard material to visualize texel density and reveal stretching; the checker serves as a diagnostic tool so you can see where squares are elongated or compressed. Second, practice making seams and creating UV shells for complex models. Treat seams like tailoring cuts so pieces can flatten without significant distortion. Third, pack shells in the 0–1 space and watch for overlapping UVs that cause texture conflicts or incorrect baking. Overlap hides mistakes and breaks ambient occlusion or normal maps. Fourth, experiment with wrong projections deliberately — apply planar to a sphere or spherical to a cylinder — to see extreme distortion; this contrast helps you learn when each projection is appropriate. These objectives pair procedural practice with quick visual tests so you can iterate confidently. After these checks, you should be able to identify whether a texture problem is a projection choice, stretching, or overlapping, and pick a clear next step to fix it.

UVs are a mapping system: each vertex on a 3D model is assigned a pair of coordinates in a two-dimensional texture space called U and V. A useful mental image is peeling an orange or unwrapping a gift box so that the curved or folded surface becomes a flat piece of material you can paint on. When you paint in a 2D program, each pixel corresponds to some UV coordinate; the renderer looks up that pixel by reading the U and V assigned to the surface point. Concretely, U is the horizontal axis and V is the vertical axis of the texture map. Without that mapping, a 2D image has no way to know which triangle or vertex it should color on a model. A common beginner misconception is thinking UVs are the texture image: they are not. They are coordinates that reference the texture. An example: a character’s eye painted in 2D will only appear in the correct place on the head if the UVs for the eye region point to that painted region in the 0-1 space. Key takeaway: separate the idea of the texture image from the coordinate map that places it. Ask yourself when checking a model: is this a texture problem or a UV mapping problem?

The 0–1 UV space is a normalized square that runs from U equals zero to U equals one and V equals zero to V equals one. This square represents the full extent of a single texture map. When artists paint in Photoshop or Substance, they assume artwork will be sampled across that square, so placing your UV shells inside 0–1 ensures the renderer fetches texture pixels predictably. For game workflows, keeping shells inside 0–1 makes atlasing and mipmapping straightforward and avoids sampling artifacts. Overlapping shells inside the 0–1 square can be intentional for mirrored symmetry, but accidental overlaps create conflicts: two different model parts will sample the same texture pixels, which breaks unique details and baked maps. A practical way to check texel distribution is to use a checker texture with repeated tiles; ideally the squares are uniformly sized across shells. A common mistake is allowing some shells to be tiny and others huge inside 0–1; that creates inconsistent texel density and visible variation in texture sharpness. Your practical rule: aim for even density and no accidental overlap inside the 0–1 square.

The UV Editor is the primary workspace for arranging UVs in Maya. Open it from Windows, UV Editors, UV Editor. Inside, you can switch selection modes—UVs, edges, faces—so you can move individual coordinates, relax edges, or select whole shells. Transformation tools behave the same as in the 3D view: move, rotate, scale. One important habit is to use a checker texture on the model to evaluate stretching; irregular squares mean non-uniform mapping. The editor also shows the 0–1 square background and lets you nudge shells back into that square if they stray. A useful workflow is: isolate a shell, choose an appropriate projection, apply the projection manipulator to align the projection, then use transform tools and, if available, unfold or relax to reduce distortion. A common error is moving UVs without watching the model—always verify the viewport while editing. Example: after cylindrical mapping a bottle, rotate and scale the rectangular side shell in the UV Editor so its checker squares are square, then pack caps separately. That loop—project, adjust, verify—is the editor workflow you’ll practice. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Planar projection flattens faces by projecting them along a single axis, like shining a flashlight perpendicular to a surface. It’s ideal for flat or mostly flat geometry such as walls, floors, or the side of a box. In Maya, select the faces or object, then choose UV, Planar Mapping and set Project From to the axis that best matches the surface orientation—Y axis for a horizontal plane, for example. Use the projection manipulator to position and scale the projected area so it covers the intended faces in the UV Editor. A common mistake is applying planar mapping to curved geometry like a sphere; that produces severe stretching and seams. A concrete example: Use planar mapping on a book cover by selecting the cover faces and projecting from the camera or axis perpendicular to the cover to produce a clean rectangular shell that maps to a flat texture image. Remember to scale and pack that shell into the 0–1 square for final texture painting.

Cylindrical projection wraps the texture around an object’s circumference, making it ideal for bottles, trunks, arms, or tree trunks.
